articles.title: Brazil election: many scientists relieved as Lula wins surprise victory
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03446-9Scientific organizations in Brazil had rallied around the incumbent president, who defied expectations to defeat his opponent in a run-off.
articles.content:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva celebrated on the evening of 25 October after coming from behind to win re-election as Brazil’s president.Credit: Maira Erlich/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won his bid for re-election on 25 October, to the relief of many scientists who feared for the future of Brazilian research if right-wing candidate Flávio Bolsonaro prevailed.

In recent weeks, some of Brazil’s leading scientific organizations, including the Brazilian Academy of Sciences in Rio de Janeiro, circulated an open letter endorsing Lula, a leftist former labour leader. It received more than 20,000 signatures. “It’s hard to express just how happy the scientific community and the Brazilian society is with Lula’s victory,” says Paulo Artaxo, a physicist at the University of São Paulo.

Science philanthropy is rising in Brazil ― upending a long tradition

Many worried that, if Bolsonaro were elected, he might slash support for Brazilian science and undermine it in the way that his father, Jair Bolsonaro, did. Jair was Brazil’s president from 2019 to 2023, and during that time, he cut science funding and expressed anti-science rhetoric during the COVID-19 pandemic, casting doubt on vaccines and promoting unproven treatments. The former president could not run for office again because he was sentenced to prison over a coup plot that he instigated after he lost his bid for re-election to Lula in 2022. He is currently serving the sentence at home because of health concerns.

It was a surprise victory yesterday for Lula, who won 51.8% of the vote compared with Flávio Bolsonaro’s 48.2%. During the first round of voting on 4 October, Lula finished behind Bolsonaro, but because neither candidate earned 50% of the total votes, a second round of voting was required. “It was very moving to watch this historic turnaround,” says Sidarta Ribeiro, a neuroscientist at the Federal University of Rio Grande do Norte in Natal.

Lula’s victory came at the end of a tumultuous election day. Shortly before the polls were meant to close, a justice in Brazil’s Supreme Court ordered them to remain open for an additional two hours. The move was requested by both Lula’s and Bolsonaro’s campaigns because of public transportation problems that made it difficult for voters to reach polling stations. In a short speech yesterday, Bolsonaro said he would not accept the results.

Support for science

This will be Lula’s fourth term overall as president of Brazil, a record for the country. He initially led Brazil for two terms between 2003 and 2011. During those terms and his current term, which started in 2023, he championed the expansion of federal universities and efforts to make higher education accessible to a broad range of Brazilians, support that he has pledged to continue. He also launched a program in 2024 that brought back about 600 Brazilian scientists to the country from international institutions, where some had gone seeking improved funding and resources.

“Lula said very clearly in his victory speech that we need to strengthen federal universities and federal institutes and significantly improve how we prepare young people for a new world of [artificial intelligence] and robotics,” Ribeiro says.

Supporters of Brazilian President Lula cheered in the streets of São Paulo on 25 October after it became clear that he had won his bid for re-election in a tight race.Credit: Rodrigo Paiva/Getty

Flávio Bolsonaro had pledged to transfer operation of Brazil’s 69 federal universities from the Ministry of Education to the Ministry of Science and Technology, which has a much smaller budget. In addition, he said he would emphasize applied sciences over basic research, which concerned some in the scientific community because “the countries that have made the greatest advances in science are those with an extremely strong foundation in basic research”, Ribeiro says.

Another major source of concern for some researchers about the election was the future of Brazil’s environmental policies. Under President Lula, deforestation in Brazil’s considerable portion of the Amazon rainforest fell to its lowest level since measurements began in 1988. Between 2019 and 2023, however, deforestation rose by almost 60% under Jair Bolsonaro, and a similar trend was expected under his son. The Amazon rainforest is considered one of the world’s largest carbon sinks, but studies suggest that increasing deforestation could cause it to release more carbon than it absorbs.

Meanwhile, Lula said during his recent campaign that he is committed to ending deforestation in Brazil by 2030, and that he would cut the country’s greenhouse-gas emissions in line with the Paris Agreement, which nations signed onto nearly a decade ago to curb climate change. “Lula’s government plan is very clear: he’ll work towards zero deforestation in the Amazon and towards implementing energy transition programs that end the use of fossil fuels in Brazil,” Artaxo says.
articles.reasoning: The article reports the re-election of Brazil's President Lula, which is seen as a positive development by the scientific community due to his commitment to supporting science, reversing previous funding cuts, and addressing critical environmental issues such as Amazon deforestation and climate change. This has broad significance for Brazil and global environmental health, with detailed context on policy impacts and scientific support.

articles.title: Chinese scientists discover “D-rex,” a giant fungus with roots stretching back 65 million years
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a giant new fungus in China that grows up to 20 inches tall and weighs nearly five pounds, making it the largest known of its kind. Dubbed “D-rex,” its evolutionary lineage appears to have emerged shortly after the dinosaurs went extinct, raising intriguing questions about how that ancient catastrophe may have shaped its evolution.
articles.content:
Scientists exploring the forests of Yunnan, China, have discovered an extraordinary giant fungus that is challenging previous assumptions about how large certain fungi can grow. The newly identified species, Dianjunus rex, produces upright reproductive structures that can reach 50 cm (20 inches) in height and weigh as much as 2.2 kg (4.9 pounds). These are the largest known fruiting bodies among fungi belonging to the phylum Ascomycota.

"This remarkable species represents a new fungal family, Dianjunaceae, and provides a rare window into the evolution of extreme fungal body forms," said Dr Indunil C Senanayake, an associate professor at the Germplasm Bank of Wild Species of the Kunming Institute of Botany in China and corresponding author of the study, published in Frontiers in Fungal Biology.

"The discovery illustrates how much fungus biodiversity remains to be discovered in East Asian forests."

A Giant Fungus Hidden in China's Forests

Researchers from the Kunming Institute of Botany encountered the unusual fungus while surveying several forest environments in Yunnan. Their fieldwork included temperate coniferous forests near Damaidi and Yipinglang, along with tropical rainforest near Nanbang.

The team spotted unusually large, whitish reproductive structures, known as 'stromata', growing from the woody roots of Chinese cork oak trees. These structures emerged from the rhizosphere, the region of soil surrounding plant roots, and appeared to belong to an unidentified member of the ascomycete fungi.

Ascomycetes make up the largest major group of fungi, with more than 64,000 recognized species. Unlike familiar mushrooms, these fungi do not produce true mushroom structures. Instead, they generate spores within tiny sac-like structures found inside or on the surfaces of their fruiting bodies.

To investigate the discovery, the scientists collected samples and preserved reference specimens in the Kunming Institute of Botany's collections. They also cultivated spores under laboratory conditions to examine the fungus's physical characteristics and sequenced its genome, including its protein-coding genes.

Meet D-Rex, a Record-Breaking Fungal Giant

The genetic analysis, together with a close examination of the fungus's physical features, revealed that the discovery represented much more than a previously unknown species. It was sufficiently different from known fungi to require the creation of a new genus and an entirely new family (Dianjunaceae) within the order Xylariales.

The researchers named the species Dianjunus rex, drawing inspiration from its impressive size and the ancient Dian kingdom. Its nickname, 'D-rex', reflects its exceptional stature among related fungi.

Its closest known relative is Graphostroma platystoma, a fungus that grows on dead hardwood throughout the Northern Hemisphere. That species is the sole representative of its own family, Graphostromataceae.

Members of the order Xylariales are known for producing a variety of specialized chemical compounds and enzymes capable of breaking down complex molecules in plants. Researchers believe similar enzymes may allow 'D-rex' to decompose dead wood and obtain nutrients from it.

A 65-Million-Year Connection to Dinosaur Extinction

One of the most intriguing findings concerns the ancient evolutionary origins of the newly identified fungal family.

Using a technique known as a 'molecular clock', the scientists compared the fungus's DNA with genomic information from hundreds of other fungi whose evolutionary histories have been established. This analysis allowed them to estimate when the Dianjunaceae family first appeared.

Their results suggest that the lineage originated approximately 65 million years ago, roughly one million years after the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction. That catastrophic event eliminated the non-avian dinosaurs along with countless other animal and plant species.

The timing raises the possibility that the enormous environmental changes following the extinction helped create favorable conditions for the ancestors of this unusual fungus.

"This timing raises an intriguing possibility. After the mass extinction, forests experienced dramatic changes, including the sudden availability of large amounts of dead plant material," said Senanayake. "For wood-associated decomposing fungi, such environmental disruption may have created new ecological opportunities."

Why Does This Fungus Grow So Large?

Another mystery is how and why Dianjunus rex evolved such an extraordinary size.

Before its discovery, the tallest known ascomycete fruiting bodies measured approximately 20 to 30 cm. The newly identified fungus can reach 50 cm, making it substantially taller than the previous record holders.

One possible explanation involves how the fungus releases and spreads its spores. By extending high above the forest floor, its reproductive structures may be better positioned to catch moving air and distribute spores through dense vegetation.

However, growing such a large structure also requires considerable energy. The researchers suggest that this unusual evolutionary strategy would be advantageous only in environments where the benefits of greater spore dispersal outweigh the resources needed for growth.

"A fruiting body which towers above surrounding vegetation and debris could have better dispersal of spores by wind in dense forests. However, such a large structure requires substantial energy investment, suggesting that this strategy likely evolved only where the ecological benefits outweighed the costs," hypothesized Senanayake.

China's Forests May Harbor More Undiscovered Fungi

The discovery also highlights how much remains unknown about fungal diversity in China's subtropical forests.

Researchers believe the region is particularly well suited to the evolution of unusual fungal species because it contains a wide variety of habitats, has experienced relatively stable climatic conditions, and supports intricate relationships among living organisms.

Despite these favorable conditions, many fungi in the region have received little scientific attention. Remote and difficult terrain complicates fieldwork, while the seasonal appearance and often hidden nature of fungal reproductive structures make some species especially difficult to locate. Historically, research has also concentrated heavily on fungi with commercial or practical value.

The scientists expect that continued exploration of these forests will uncover additional species, potentially revealing more unexpected forms and evolutionary histories.

"This region combines exceptional habitat heterogeneity, climatic stability, and complex biotic interactions that promote fungal diversification. Historically, however, fungal diversity in these ecosystems has been underestimated due to logistical difficulties in field sampling, the seasonal and cryptic nature of fungal fruiting, and a historical emphasis on economically important fungi," said Senanayake.
articles.reasoning: The discovery of a giant new fungus species with a unique evolutionary lineage provides significant scientific insight into biodiversity and fungal evolution, highlighting the rich, underexplored fungal diversity in China's forests. This has broad environmental and ecological implications, expanding knowledge of ecosystem complexity and evolutionary history following a major extinction event.

articles.title: California has a plan for El Niño’s torrential rain: Save it for later
articles.content:
Something ominous just hit California: rain.

The life-giving water that normally hydrates people and crops is bringing an aura of dread this autumn, thanks to the strongest El Niño ever recorded. While the phenomenon causes severe drought and heat in many parts of the world, historically it’s brought extraordinary rainfall to the Golden State. The monstrous El Niño of 1997 and 1998, for instance, caused widespread flooding and debris flows (made not just of water and dirt, but big chunks of rock), destroying property and killing residents.

The state can’t stop rain from falling, so in the last few decades it has been renegotiating its relationship with precipitation. As climate change makes California whiplash from years of intense drought to years of intense rain, water agencies have been capturing as much H2O as they can to reduce reliance on using canals to bring it in from afar. That’s set the state up to avoid at least some flooding as this El Niño takes hold and bank the bounty for the dry spells to come.

“Heavy storms can affect regional infrastructure, construction schedules, and areas vulnerable to debris flow or power disruptions,” said a spokesperson with the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power in a statement provided to Grist. “However, these rain events also present a significant opportunity. Stormwater capture is a critical pillar of LADWP’s long-term plan to reduce reliance on purchased imported water.”

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The threat isn’t just more rain overall, but the way it arrives. If one storm hits, water can build up and flood, but some of it will soak into the ground, preventing further inundation. But if a succession of storms rolls through, the soils get saturated. “Even one can be very big and impactful,” said Steven Springhorn, supervising engineering geologist in the California Department of Water Resources’ sustainable groundwater management office. “But if they start to come in a series, that’s where you start to get into some situations where you have a lot of excess water.”

Water, like any material thing, moves through time and space but brings unique challenges in both realms. For one, it’s heavy, so channeling it requires using pumps or gravity, like when draining water out of a reservoir. And for humans, at least, the rain’s timing isn’t always ideal: A lot can fall at once, or it doesn’t fall for months on end.

To address the timing problem, California operates nearly 1,500 reservoirs. But that creates a challenge with space, as the dams can only hold back so much water — during especially wet winters, the reservoirs occasionally release water to keep from overfilling or even breaking apart. That’s to say nothing of the plethora of environmental harms that come from damming rivers, like destroying migratory routes for fishes.

So in recent years, California has been turning its attention underground, to its sprawling aquifers. In 2014, the state passed the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act, which requires local water agencies to tackle the crisis of dwindling subterranean supplies. California has long been extracting an unsustainable amount of groundwater, due in part to droughts exacerbated by climate change. The issue is particularly acute in the agricultural Central Valley, where farmers have drawn so much groundwater that aquifers have been collapsing like empty plastic bottles, causing the land to sink by nearly 30 feet.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

But that problem is also an opportunity. Whereas the state’s major reservoirs currently hold around 21 million acre-feet of water — that is, the amount it’d take to cover an acre in a foot of the stuff — its land could hold something like a billion acre-feet underground, according to Michael Kiparsky, director of the Wheeler Water Institute at the University of California, Berkeley. “So the potential room for storage is immense,” Kiparsky said. “The enticing question is: Is there a way to grab those flood flows before they flow out to sea, and hold them underground, and therefore expand our capacity?”

That strategy is known as managed aquifer recharge, which tweaks how water moves through space and time. California water agencies, for instance, have been diverting excess rainfall into big dirt bowls on the landscape. This slows it down, allowing it to seep into the underlying aquifer. “If that fills up, then they go and talk to the growers in the area and see if there could be opportunities to put that water on agricultural land,” Springhorn said.

Whether it’s in basins or on fields, the water moves underground where, as a bonus, it’s not lost to the evaporation that inevitably occurs in a reservoir. When summer rolls around, water managers and farmers can pump that groundwater back up. Indeed, in an average year, this subterranean stash provides about 40 percent of California’s supply. “But in a drought, it makes up even more,” Springhorn said. “So that’s why we want to use the wet years, and the excess water that might be there, to replenish the aquifers so that there’s more there year to year.”

As a bonus, managed aquifer recharge can boost biodiversity. California has lost 95 percent of its wetlands, which used to mitigate flooding and provide critical habitat, especially for migrating birds. To help restore them, a Nature Conservancy project called BirdReturns incentivizes farmers in the Central Valley to flood their acreage, replicating the erstwhile ecosystems. “The local landowners can make a profit off doing a service for this really valued part of ecology,” Kiparsky said, “and it functions also as a groundwater-recharge project.”

But what about the state’s cities? Like metropolises the world over, California’s were designed to move water into sewers and out of the built environment quickly. But as climate change intensifies rainfall — a warmer atmosphere by default holds more moisture — wastewater systems are struggling to keep up. “The gray infrastructure that we built in the 20th century was really built for a climate that is no longer here,” said Edith de Guzman, a water equity and adaptation policy cooperative extension specialist at the University of California, Los Angeles. “We can’t just engineer our way out of the problems — we need to actually kind of reverse-engineer a little bit and think about the way that nature does things.”

Simply put: Gray infrastructure like concrete is a liability, whereas green and brown spaces are assets. So in 2018, Los Angeles County voters passed a tax of 2.5 cents per square foot of impermeable land, like driveways, raising nearly $300 million annually. That finances preserving local watersheds and developing stormwater-capture projects, helping the region pioneer a better way to manage urban water by getting “spongier.” As it develops roadside gardens and retrofits public parks, Los Angeles creates more spaces for the liquid to soak into the ground. It’s also built several spreading grounds, a series of bowls where water accumulates.

All told, the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power said that in the 2025-2026 water year, it captured around 37 billion gallons of stormwater. (The average resident uses around 100 gallons a day.) “While intense downpours require active management, they allow us to maximize local groundwater replenishment and capture as much precious rainfall as possible when it arrives,” said the spokesperson for the LADWP.

By building out as much spongy infrastructure as possible, California cities like L.A. better prepare themselves not just for the aquatic ravages of El Niño, but for the hotter summers ahead. Green spaces significantly cool the neighborhoods lucky enough to have them, while urban farms go a step further in producing nutritious food for residents. “The psychological and societal benefits,” de Guzman said, “are really not something to be ignored in this era of ever-increasing needs for us to have more connection and more reasons to celebrate where we live, rather than reasons to stay on our phones indoors with our air-conditioning on.”

articles.personality_title: California turns heavy El Niño rains into a water-saving opportunity
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – California often faces extreme weather swings, from droughts to heavy rains. The strongest El Niño ever recorded is expected to bring heavy rain this year, which can cause flooding and damage.

**What happened** – Instead of just trying to stop floods, California has been preparing to catch and save the rainwater. The state uses nearly 1,500 reservoirs and also stores water underground in large aquifers. They slow down rainwater in special basins and let it soak into the ground, so it doesn’t flood cities or farms. Los Angeles, for example, has built parks and gardens that soak up rain, capturing billions of gallons each year.

**Impact** – This method helps reduce floods, saves water for dry times, and supports nature. Storing water underground avoids the evaporation that happens in reservoirs. It also helps restore wetlands that many birds depend on. In cities, green spaces cool neighborhoods and improve quality of life, making urban areas better prepared for climate change.

**What’s next step** – California will keep expanding these water-saving projects, including more underground storage and “spongy” urban spaces. This approach aims to handle future storms better and support farmers, wildlife, and city residents through changing weather patterns.

**One-sentence takeaway** – California is turning heavy rains from El Niño into a valuable water resource by capturing and storing it underground and in green urban spaces to prepare for future dry spells and floods.
articles.personality_title_fr: La Californie transforme les fortes pluies d’El Niño en une ressource précieuse
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La Californie connaît souvent des changements climatiques extrêmes, entre sécheresses et fortes pluies. Le plus fort El Niño jamais enregistré devrait apporter cette année de fortes pluies, pouvant causer des inondations et des dégâts.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Plutôt que de simplement lutter contre les inondations, la Californie se prépare à capter et conserver l’eau de pluie. L’État utilise près de 1 500 réservoirs et stocke aussi l’eau sous terre dans de grandes nappes phréatiques. Ils ralentissent les eaux de pluie dans des bassins spéciaux pour qu’elles s’infiltrent dans le sol, évitant ainsi les inondations dans les villes ou les fermes. À Los Angeles, par exemple, des parcs et jardins absorbent la pluie, capturant chaque année des milliards de gallons.

**Impact** – Cette méthode réduit les inondations, économise de l’eau pour les périodes sèches et soutient la nature. Stocker l’eau sous terre évite l’évaporation des réservoirs. Cela aide aussi à restaurer des zones humides indispensables à de nombreux oiseaux. En ville, les espaces verts rafraîchissent les quartiers et améliorent la qualité de vie, préparant mieux les zones urbaines au changement climatique.

**Prochaine étape** – La Californie va continuer à développer ces projets d’économie d’eau, avec davantage de stockage souterrain et d’espaces urbains « éponges ». Cette stratégie vise à mieux gérer les futures tempêtes et à soutenir agriculteurs, faune et habitants face aux changements climatiques.

**Résumé en une phrase** – La Californie transforme les fortes pluies d’El Niño en une ressource précieuse en les captant et stockant sous terre et dans des espaces verts urbains pour mieux affronter les sécheresses et inondations futures.
articles.personality_title_es: California convierte las fuertes lluvias de El Niño en un recurso valioso
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – California suele enfrentar cambios climáticos extremos, desde sequías hasta lluvias intensas. El fenómeno El Niño más fuerte registrado traerá este año lluvias fuertes que pueden causar inundaciones y daños.

**Qué pasó** – En lugar de solo luchar contra las inundaciones, California se ha preparado para captar y guardar el agua de lluvia. El estado usa casi 1,500 embalses y también almacena agua bajo tierra en grandes acuíferos. Ralentizan la lluvia en cuencas especiales para que se filtre al suelo, evitando inundaciones en ciudades y granjas. Por ejemplo, Los Ángeles ha creado parques y jardines que absorben la lluvia, capturando miles de millones de galones cada año.

**Impacto** – Este método ayuda a reducir inundaciones, guardar agua para tiempos secos y apoyar la naturaleza. Guardar agua bajo tierra evita la evaporación que ocurre en los embalses. También ayuda a restaurar humedales que necesitan muchas aves. En las ciudades, los espacios verdes enfrían los vecindarios y mejoran la calidad de vida, preparando mejor las áreas urbanas para el cambio climático.

**Próximo paso** – California seguirá ampliando estos proyectos para ahorrar agua, con más almacenamiento subterráneo y espacios urbanos esponjosos. Esta estrategia busca manejar mejor futuras tormentas y apoyar a agricultores, animales y residentes frente a los cambios climáticos.

**Resumen en una frase** – California convierte las fuertes lluvias de El Niño en un recurso valioso al captarlas y almacenarlas bajo tierra y en espacios verdes urbanos para prepararse mejor para sequías e inundaciones futuras.

articles.title: Tiny zebra-striped bee in West a 'huge surprise'
articles.summary: A zebra-striped bee is seen in Somerset for the first time, offering hope in restored saltmarshes.
articles.content:
A tiny zebra-striped bee, usually found along England's south and east coasts, has made an unexpected journey to the West Country.

The rare sea aster mining bee has been spotted at Steart Marshes in Somerset by naturalist Nigel Phillips, who said the find "was a huge surprise".

The Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust said saltmarsh restoration work at the nature reserve had helped create the perfect home for the newcomer.

The charity says the discovery shows how rare species and wildlife can thrive by restoring coastal habitats.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on the positive environmental impact of saltmarsh restoration leading to the unexpected arrival and thriving of a rare bee species, indicating successful habitat restoration with broader ecological benefits.
articles.personality_title: Rare zebra-striped bee spotted for first time in Somerset saltmarsh
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The sea aster mining bee is a small, striped bee usually found only on England’s south and east coasts. It lives in special coastal areas where sea aster plants grow.

**What happened** – In Somerset’s Steart Marshes, naturalist Nigel Phillips saw this rare bee for the first time in the West Country. This surprise sighting happened because the area has been restored to bring back saltmarsh habitats.

**Impact** – The saltmarsh restoration helped create a good home for the bee, showing that bringing back natural habitats can support rare wildlife. This is important because it means efforts to fix damaged environments can help animals that are hard to find.

**What’s next step** – The discovery encourages more work to restore coastal areas, which could help more rare species return. Scientists and conservation groups will likely keep monitoring the marshes to see what other wildlife comes back.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Restoring saltmarshes in Somerset has allowed a rare zebra-striped bee to appear, proving that habitat restoration supports wildlife recovery.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une rare abeille rayée zébrée observée pour la première fois dans les marais salants du Somerset
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – L’abeille fouisseuse de l’aster maritime est une petite abeille rayée que l’on trouve habituellement uniquement sur les côtes sud et est de l’Angleterre. Elle vit dans des zones côtières spéciales où pousse l’aster maritime.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Dans les marais de Steart au Somerset, le naturaliste Nigel Phillips a vu pour la première fois cette abeille rare dans l’ouest du pays. Cette observation surprenante a eu lieu grâce à la restauration des habitats des marais salants.

**Impact** – La restauration des marais salants a permis de créer un bon habitat pour l’abeille, montrant que la remise en état des environnements naturels peut soutenir des espèces rares. C’est important car cela prouve que réparer des milieux endommagés peut aider des animaux difficiles à trouver.

**Prochaine étape** – Cette découverte incite à poursuivre les travaux de restauration des zones côtières, ce qui pourrait permettre à d’autres espèces rares de revenir. Les scientifiques et les associations de protection surveilleront probablement les marais pour voir quels autres animaux reviennent.

**Phrase clé** – La restauration des marais salants du Somerset a permis à une rare abeille rayée zébrée d’apparaître, prouvant que la restauration des habitats aide la faune à se rétablir.
articles.personality_title_es: Abeja rayada rara avistada por primera vez en los marismas del Somerset
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La abeja minera de aster marítimo es una pequeña abeja rayada que generalmente se encuentra solo en las costas sur y este de Inglaterra. Vive en áreas costeras especiales donde crecen las plantas de aster marítimo.

**Qué pasó** – En los marismas de Steart en Somerset, el naturalista Nigel Phillips vio por primera vez esta abeja rara en el oeste del país. Esta sorpresa ocurrió gracias a la restauración de los hábitats de marisma.

**Impacto** – La restauración de la marisma ayudó a crear un buen hogar para la abeja, mostrando que devolver la naturaleza puede apoyar a la vida silvestre rara. Esto es importante porque demuestra que arreglar ambientes dañados puede ayudar a animales difíciles de encontrar.

**Próximo paso** – El descubrimiento anima a continuar con el trabajo de restauración de áreas costeras, lo que podría ayudar a que más especies raras regresen. Científicos y grupos de conservación probablemente seguirán vigilando las marismas para ver qué otros animales vuelven.

**Frase clave** – Restaurar las marismas en Somerset permitió la aparición de una rara abeja rayada, demostrando que la restauración del hábitat apoya la recuperación de la vida silvestre.
